articles.headline: Last Sabbath
articles.summary: We were at Bethel Church for the first time in nearly three months, owing to our absence, and heard Rev. Joseph H. Smith preach from Isaiah iii. 10. We found Bethel Church without the Elder who was appointed at the last annual Conference. It seems that he and some of the people did not agree very well, and he has resigned. Rev. Stephen Smith holds the charge until the Bishop appoints some one else. We hear that he expects to appoint Elder Schureman to the charge. Rev. J. P. Campbell speaks of getting a chaplaincy in some one of the colored regiments.

articles.headline: Sixth U. S. Colored Regiment at Camp William Penn
articles.summary: This regiment has not been ordered to move yet. They are still under drill by Col. Wagner and Captain G. P. Riley. This gentleman has been chaplain in a regiment out in Kentucky, and has been promoted to the position of a Captain. The 7th regt. (as printed) is filling up fast, and have now, we believe, four or five hundred already, and they have decided to put up barracks for the fall and winter.

articles.headline: Mr. Burris at Sansom St. Hall
articles.summary: Last Thursday night we were present, and found the hall crowded. Mr. Burris and his troupe were performing nicely. Some of the audience got so happy that some men rose up in front of the audience and commenced prancing, some would call it dancing; we thought that was very much out of place on that occasion. Mrs. Burris, who had a cake and ice cream stand, treated us to a good dish of cream and cake.

articles.headline: For the Christian Recorder (letter from Philadelphia on emancipation and colored soldiers)
articles.author: M
articles.summary: Phila., Sept. 26th, 1863. Mr. Editor: This is the first time that I ever attempted to mar the surface of your sheet by an insertion. I have read your paper with great carefulness. Since the President's emancipation proclamation every negro within the limits of these United States is free. The editor's 'Take Notice' on the same page says the piece is published for the author but that no more will appear unless he gives his full name.

articles.headline: Camp William Penn
articles.summary: We were out there on Wednesday last, and found the place is alive with troops, and while we were there a squad of men were brought from the city. We don't know whether the 6th regiment will go until the other is full or not.

articles.headline: Colored Troops' Parade in Philadelphia
articles.summary: The 6th United States colored regiment, and four companies of the eighth regiment, on last Saturday, the 3d inst., came in from Camp William Penn, and formed a line on Master St., right resting on Fourth, facing south, and marched down Fourth to Brown, up Brown to Sixth, down Sixth to Arch, up Arch to Twentieth, down Twentieth to Chestnut, down Chestnut to Eighteenth, down Eighteenth to Walnut, down Walnut to Seventeenth, down Seventeenth to Pine, down Pine to Broad, up Broad to Chestnut, down Chestnut to Third, down Third to Walnut, down Walnut to Dock, down Dock to Second, down Second to Washington, and down Washington to the Refreshment Saloon. No troops ever passed through the streets of Philadelphia that made a better appearance.

articles.author: S. Hutchinson and J. Cromwell
articles.summary: Mr. Editor: It is with a feeling of awe that we take up our pens to write a few lines for the 'Christian Recorder;' and though we are not personally acquainted with you, yet we think we can safely trespass on your columns, by writing a few lines on the above subject. articles.headline: Died (Sister Margaret Moore)
articles.author: Edward Laws
articles.summary: Mr. Editor: Please give this a place in the Recorder. The death of one of our sisters, who departed in the triumphs of faith. On Sabbath morning, about 9 o'clock, the 27th of September, she crossed her hands on her breast, and went to sleep in Jesus. On Tuesday afternoon her funeral took place, at which time I preached her funeral sermon. Sister Margaret Moore leaves behind her a dear husband, and three small children. She was aged 22 years; she had been a member of the Church about five years. Her husband's name is James Moore. No place is given.

articles.headline: The Great Secret: Why Colored People are not Accommodated in the Street Cars of Philadelphia. Let Every Body Read It
articles.summary: The companies have generally employed as drivers and conductors of the street cars, the enemies of the colored people and those who are generally in sympathy with the rebellion. This can no longer be disguised. Let any honest man examine the most of the drivers, and they will soon learn what influence the drivers and conductors used to have Judge Woodward elected Governor of Pennsylvania. They generally have no regard for a respectable colored man or woman; but they will take your money, and then you may ride anywhere in front. On last Wednesday morning we had been down to the foot of Washington Street, and on our way back we thought we could take the cars and ride up to Chestnut Street, which we did. We took car No. 48 on the front.
people: passenger abused on the front of a Sixth Street car; conductor kept his ten cent piece

articles.headline: The Departure of the 6th U. S. Colored Regiment
articles.summary: On last Wednesday morning, the Sixth Colored Regiment of the U. S. came in from Camp William Penn, and marched down Chestnut St. to the head quarters all equipped for the war; from there they marched down to Second St., and thence to Washington St., and to the refreshment saloon, where dinner was prepared for them all at the union saloon, and at the cooper shop, where they all fared sumptuously. About 5 o'clock, P. M., they commenced to embark on board the steamer Conqueror.

Bishop Nazrey was just in the act of reading the hymn for the morning service, and he gave us a very good sermon; after which we administered the Lord's Supper. In the afternoon the Rev. W. H. Jones (Panorama) preached a very good and appropriate sermon. In the evening we went to Bethel and heard a minister who hailed from Baltimore, Maryland.

articles.headline: For the Christian Recorder (the new Elder introduced at Bethel)
articles.summary: Last Sabbath, at Bethel Church, occurred one of those incidents which I believe never occurred before in the history of the church since its organization: the introduction of a new Elder in the midst of the conference year. The circumstances leading to it are, perhaps, too well known to need further reference. The service of the morning was interesting, and drew together a tolerably large congregation. Bishop Nazrey was present. The new Elder, Rev. W. D. W. Schureman, preached from Matt. 21: 28, 'Son, go work to-day.' Bishop Payne preached, or rather presented, the claims of the Wilberforce University at 3 o'clock in the afternoon, to a very full house.

articles.headline: Letter from the 6th United States Colored Troops
articles.author: G. P. Riley
articles.summary: Yorktown, Virginia, October 19th, 1863. Mr. Editor: Sir, we arrived at this place last night, after a very tedious and by no means agreeable voyage, of four days and nights. We remained at Philadelphia eighteen hours after we embarked; we cast anchor for the night, and the next day (Friday) got to the break-water with a stormy sea before us. The fresh water had run out and salt water was distilled; on Sabbath morning, the 18th, we found ourselves at Fortress Monroe, ran up to this place, disembarked, marched up through the fort and encamped on the plains of Yorktown. Capt. G. P. Riley.

articles.headline: A Flying Visit to Washington and Georgetown, D. C.

We struck a bee-line for the hospitable mansion of Brother Wright. Arrangements were at once made for us to preach, on the following Sabbath, at Union Bethel, under the care of Rev. James A. Handy. At five o'clock, P. M., we left Baltimore for Philadelphia, our own homestead, arriving at half past ten o'clock at night.

articles.summary: We visited Brother Cooper on last Sabbath, at the opening of his Mission, at Broad and Lombard Sts., and must say that we were much pleased both at the service and at the number in attendance. Brother James Frisby preached at 3 o'clock, and we must say that he seemed thoroughly imbued with the spirit of missions. We never heard him more practical.

articles.headline: The Sick and Wounded Colored Soldiers
articles.summary: We think the Colored Soldiers do not receive that attention from their colored friends that their sufferings and patriotism demand. We do not know, as a general thing, the amount of relief or aid rendered in this direction by our people, or we would cheerfully give them credit for it. [The editor asks for weekly meetings to relieve the colored soldiers in the hospitals and camps, and for books, tracts and religious papers; amounts contributed will be published.]

articles.author: Richard H. Black
articles.summary: Dear Sir: Having often promised myself to write to you, at one time I had almost accomplished the prompted desire, but the changes made soon after, frustrated my plans. articles.headline: Bethel Church (repairs)
articles.summary: This church is now undergoing extensive repairs, at an outlay of some twelve hundred dollars or more, and the congregation in the meantime worship in the basement, and expect to resume services in the main audience room by the first of December. They wish their church to present a respectable appearance by the time the General Conference assembles.

articles.headline: Respectable Colored Persons Wanted
articles.summary: There are such things as distinctions among mankind; for there are the poor and the rich, the good and the bad, the ignorant and the wise, the respectful and the disrespectful: but we ought certainly to protest against the word respectable in the manner in which it is applied to colored people. [An editorial against advertisements worded 'Respectable colored persons wanted, or admitted.']

articles.headline: Presentation of a Flag (Sansom St. Hall)

The hall was filled to overflowing with both colored and white people, on which occasion the presentation of a flag to the 3d Regiment of the United States Colored troops took place. The flag was painted by our excellent and gentlemanly Mr. Bowser, who is a colored man and an artist No. 1. It was prepared by the special order of our patriotic colored ladies of Philadelphia, who contributed funds for that purpose.

articles.summary: Dear Friend: I now sit down to write to you, asking you if the people of the city of Philadelphia have altogether forgotten the 3d Regiment of United States Colored Troops. B, 3d United States Colored Troops, Morris Island, S.C., October 23d, 1863. He asks Philadelphians for books, papers, preserves and tobacco for the sick in hospital, reports the regiment's work in the trenches before Forts Wagner and Gregg, ten men killed and over twenty wounded, and praises Colonel Tilghman.]

T., and especially to that part of it which solicits sympathy for the sick and wounded in the hospital. Let our good friends contribute those articles which are needed and will be of great benefit to the suffering soldiers. Also send them books and religious papers to read.

articles.headline: Editorial Correspondence: Our Stay in New York and Brooklyn (with a passage on the exclusion of colored people from the Philadelphia passenger cars)
articles.summary: The principal thoroughfares of New York city and Brooklyn present to the eye of the observer one continued and living stream of human souls, bustling along and surging to and fro in endless crowds. [The editor, travelling to Brooklyn, New York and Boston, contrasts the East with Philadelphia: there 'you come to the street cars, the driver will hold up his hand to you, stops for you, and you step on, walk inside, and the ladies and gentlemen will make room for you'; 'I am sorry to say that this is not the case in Philadelphia and other portions of the State; for if a respectable colored man should enter one of the passenger cars in this city, where white folks were, he would probably be maltreated.' Dated at the close Monday morning, November 2d.]

articles.headline: The Pay of Colored Soldiers
articles.summary: We have received information several times of the fact, through some of our colored soldiers, that, though they perform just as much manual labor as the white soldier, and, in some cases, even more, an attempt has been made to pay them but seven dollars per month for their services, which they very properly refused to accept and demanded the same pay as white soldiers. It would be manifest injustice in the Government to offer the colored soldier seven, while the white receives thirteen dollars, besides the large bounties given.

articles.headline: From Our Soldiers (Third U. S. C. Troops, Morris Island; medals of honor; pay refused)
articles.author: H. S. Harmon
articles.summary: Camp Third U. S. C. Troops, Morris Island, December 1863. Dear Friend: In my last letter I endeavored to bring before the public some facts concerning our sick and wounded comrades, but now I wish to say something concerning those who need nothing but the sympathies and hearty co-operation of friends at home. General Gillmore promised a medal of honor to two men of every company in the regiment for bravery shown before Fort Wagner; in our company they were Privates George Reed and William Roberts, both Lancaster County boys. Signed Sergeant H. S. Harmon.

events.location: Bethel Church, Philadelphia
events.description: First printed preaching plan for Bethel after Rev. J. P. Campbell's resignation: 10 a.m. Rev. A. L. Stanford; 3 p.m. Rev. Wm. Alston; 7 1/2 p.m. Rev. Elisha Weaver. Signed Rev. Stephen Smith, Elder in Charge. The editorial 'Last Sabbath' in the same issue says Smith holds the charge until the Bishop appoints, and that Elder Schureman is expected to be appointed.

events.name: Prof. Wm. H. Jones's Panoramic Exhibition at Bethel
events.location: Bethel Church, Philadelphia
events.description: Panorama exhibited on 'last Thursday evening' (Oct. 1) to over five hundred persons; to be repeated at Bethel on the next Thursday evening (Oct. 8) at 8 o'clock.

events.name: Mr. Burris's concert at Sansom Street Hall
events.location: Sansom Street Hall, Philadelphia
events.description: Concert by Mr. Burris and his troupe on 'last Thursday night' before a crowded hall; the editor attended, left at half past 9 to marry a couple at his house, and returned until after 10. He objected to some men 'prancing' in front of the audience. Mrs. Burris kept a cake and ice cream stand.

events.name: Camp meeting and quarterly meeting, A. M. E. Church, Woodbury, N. J.
events.location: A. M. E. Church, Woodbury, N. J.
events.description: Camp meeting to commence Saturday, Oct. 10, with the quarterly meeting, and continue one week; preaching Saturday evening, three or four times on the Sabbath, and afternoons and evenings through the week. Notice signed by the preacher in charge, read as Jacob P. Jay [VERIFY], 'subject to James Hollen' [VERIFY].

events.name: Harvest home for the church at Salem, N. J.
events.location: Salem, N. J.
events.description: Harvest home held 'on the 3d inst.' for the benefit of the Salem church; addresses by Rev. J. Woodlin, Brother J. P. Jay and Rev. Wm. H. Jones (who 'could sing like a nightingale'); $81.08 realized. Reported by the pastor of Salem Circuit, read as J. Hollen [VERIFY].

events.name: Parade of the 6th U.S. Colored Regiment and four companies of the 8th through Philadelphia
events.location: Philadelphia: Master St. at Fourth to the Union Volunteer Refreshment Saloon, foot of Washington St.
events.description: On Saturday, Oct. 3, the 6th United States colored regiment and four companies of the eighth came in from Camp William Penn, formed on Master St., right resting on Fourth, and marched by Fourth, Brown, Sixth, Arch, Twentieth, Chestnut, Eighteenth, Walnut, Seventeenth, Pine, Broad, Chestnut, Third, Walnut, Dock, Second and Washington to the Refreshment Saloon. The editor praises their appearance, reports loyal citizens cheering with handkerchiefs and flags, a bystander at Third and Walnut rebuked for calling the colors 'the flag of distress', and offensive remarks heard only between South and Lombard Sts. on the east side of the market house. The regiment was fed at the Union Volunteer Refreshment Saloon (committee of managers named: chairman Mr. Arad Barrows; recording sec. J. B. Wade; treasurer B. S. Brown; steward J. T. Williams; physician E. Ward; cor. sec. Robt. R. Corson; ladies Mrs. Mary Grover, Mrs. Hannah Smith, Mrs. Priscilla Grover, Miss Sarah Holland, Mrs. Emily Mason, Mrs. Mary Green, Miss Catherine Bailey). Four companies of the 8th and the officers dined at the Cooper Shop Refreshment Saloon; the editor reports talk that its committee had voted not to feed or wait on negro soldiers, but that when the 6th came down they opened the doors, and Mr. Cooper told him the soldiers behaved as well as any troops he had fed. Cooper Shop committee as printed: president W. M. Cooper; vice presidents A. S. Simpson and W. Sprole; rec. secretary W. M. Maull; cor. secretary E. J. Herety; treasurer A. M. Simpson; store-keeper W. H. Dennis. The saloon committees are white citizens and are not linked.

events.name: Grand Tabernacle of Love and Charity: hearing of the King Solomon Tabernacle No. 6 dispute
events.location: Philadelphia Institute, Lombard Street below Eighth, Philadelphia
events.description: Proceedings published by a committee of the Grand Tabernacle of Pennsylvania, Independent Order of Brothers and Sisters of Love and Charity, answering the Q3 notice that J. P. B. Eddy and the Longfellows had been expelled. On Sept. 14, 1863 the Grand Worthy Superior, William Cooper, convened the Grand Tabernacle (notice given in the Christian Recorder and The Press) on the petition of Joshua P. B. Eddy, William H. Longfellow and others. A committee of disinterested members was appointed: Richard H. Gleaves (Olive Branch Tab. No. 8), T. Manning (Celestial No. 7), Henry M. Cropper (Atheneum No. 13; printed 'Henry H Cropper' on p. 2), Caroline E. Gilbert (Jerusalem No. 1; printed 'Cornelia E. Gilbert' elsewhere), Margaret Murray (Atheneum No. 13), E. L. Freeman (Celestial No. 7), F. C. Revels (Atheneum No. 13; also printed F. B. and F. O.). The committee met at a house in Pine Street on Thursday afternoon the 17th; the plaintiff, David W. Brown, refused to appear; witnesses Joseph A. Scott (Rodman Street), Harriet Mills (Vine Street) and Hannah Mercer (Rodman Street) testified that twelve legal beneficial members met on June 4 at their room, 3d floor of the New Masonic Hall, South 11th Street below Pine. The minute book showed Elizabeth P. Longfellow, Treasurer, Israel P. Mills, Financial Scribe, and Mary E. Carpenter, Recording Scribe, duly elected Feb. 20, 1863 for six months. The defendants were honorably discharged (report signed R. H. Gleaves, chairman; Elizabeth L. L. Freeman, sec. pro tem.; Thaddeus A. Manning, M. Murray, Cornelia Gilbert, F. C. Revels, Henry M. Cropper). At a further call on Sept. 18 the Grand Tabernacle endorsed William Cooper as Grand Worthy Superior (an article of Sept. 1863 had announced James H. Smith as Grand Worthy Superior, chosen by a rival meeting at the Masonic Hall), and resolved that the body which met at the Masonic Hall, South 11th St., on June 18 and Aug. 6 was illegal, and that the publication that J. P. B. Eddy, Israel J. (sic) Mills, Mary E. Carpenter, Elizabeth P. Longfellow and William H. Longfellow had been expelled was 'a base and wicked falsehood' meant to damage their business. Speakers: William H. Longfellow ('a Grand Mob'), Richard H. Gleaves, Rev. Joshua P. B. Eddy. Committee on publication: William H. Longfellow, Thaddeus A. Manning, Elizabeth L. L. Freeman, William Cooper, Amanda Gustus.
attendees: chairman of committee, Olive Branch Tabernacle No. 8
committee, secretary pro tem., Celestial Tabernacle No. 7
Financial Scribe, King Solomon Tabernacle No. 6
Recording Scribe, King Solomon Tabernacle No. 6

events.name: Grand Tabernacle of Love and Charity, annual meeting at West Chester broken up
events.location: West Chester, Pa.
events.description: As recounted in the committee's publication: at West Chester on Sept. 4, 1863, members claiming to be King Solomon Tabernacle No. 6 objected to J. P. B. Eddy and William H. Longfellow being present; the Grand Worthy Superior, William Cooper, ruled he had no official notice of any expulsion and was threatened with violence; he declared the proceedings illegal and withdrew. Printed list of those who withdrew: Wm. Cooper, G. W. S.; Henry Gilbert, D. G. W. S.; Wm. H. Longfellow, G. W. R. S.; John S. Rock, of Boston, attorney at law; Rev. Peter Gardener; Daniel Thomas (elsewhere 'David Thomas'); Mary Brown; F. C. Revels; Nathaniel Derham (elsewhere N. L. / A. L. Durham, spelling unclear); J. Manning; Mary E. Corsey [VERIFY]; Julia A. Brown; Joseph Scott; Harriet Mills; J. P. B. Eddy. Bro. Henry Brooks then took the chair and those remaining re-organized and elected officers, which the committee calls illegal.
attendees: excluded member (printed J. P. B. Eddy)
took the chair after the withdrawal

events.name: Union A. M. E. Church, Coates St.: quarterly meeting appointments
events.location: Union A. M. E. Church, Coates St., Philadelphia
events.description: Sacramental discourse by the pastor Sunday Oct. 11 at 3 p.m.; Quarterly Conference Tuesday evening Oct. 13; General Class Friday evening Oct. 16; quarterly meeting Sunday Oct. 18; love-feast Monday evening Oct. 19 (doors open 7, close 8). Signed A. L. Stanford, Minister in Charge.

events.name: Streetcar discrimination: the editor denied a seat on the front of car No. 48
events.location: City passenger railway, from the foot of Washington Street to Chestnut Street, Philadelphia
events.description: On 'last Wednesday morning' (Oct. 14, the day the 6th U.S.C.T. embarked) the editor of the Recorder (Rev. Elisha Weaver), returning from the foot of Washington Street, rode up to Chestnut Street standing on the front platform of car No. 48 [VERIFY number], the only place allowed to colored riders. Tired, and seeing white passengers frequently sit on the driver's seat while the driver stood, he asked to sit awhile; the driver refused ('you will be in the way of passengers getting on front'; 'it's against the rules of the company') and rang for the conductor, who repeated that it was against the rules, took the seat off and carried it into the car, 'but he took good care to keep the money'. The editor offered to get off if his money was returned. He charges that the companies employ as drivers and conductors enemies of the colored people who worked to elect Judge Woodward governor, and contrasts New York, Pittsburgh, Brooklyn and Boston, where colored passengers are accommodated.
attendees: the editor; refused a seat on the front platform (Rev.)

events.name: Streetcar discrimination: Mr. William Anthony abused and short-changed on a Sixth Street car
events.location: Sixth Street passenger railway car, Philadelphia
events.description: Reported in the editorial 'The Great Secret': 'only a week or so ago' a very respectable colored man, Mr. William Anthony, 'well known in the city', got on the front of the Sixth Street cars where two or three ruffians were standing; between them and the driver they blackguarded him and almost struck him. The conductor came forward for his fare; he gave a ten cent piece and asked for the change; the conductor said 'You only gave me five cents' and kept it all. The rowdies, driver and conductor all turned upon him and would have hurt him very badly but for some passengers who interfered. No exact date is given (early October 1863).
attendees: passenger abused and denied his change

events.name: Departure of the 6th U.S. Colored Regiment from Philadelphia
events.location: Chestnut St. to the refreshment saloons and the dock at the foot of Washington St., Philadelphia
events.description: On Wednesday morning, Oct. 14, the Sixth Colored Regiment came in from Camp William Penn and marched down Chestnut St. to the head quarters fully equipped, then to Second St. and Washington St. to the refreshment saloons, where dinner was given at the Union saloon and the Cooper Shop. An immense crowd of white and colored followed. About 5 p.m. they began to embark on the steamer Conqueror, which left the dock at the foot of Washington St. at 10 minutes past six; three cheers for the Union, for Governor Curtin, for Colonel Wagner and for Captain Sullivan of the steamer; the men sang 'John Brown's body'. Mothers, sisters, fathers and wives stood in tears. Ordered to Fortress Monroe to report to Major-General Foster. Field officers as printed: Colonel J. W. Ames, formerly captain in the 11th Infantry; Lieutenant Colonel E. C. Royce; Major J. B. Kiddoo, formerly colonel of the 137th Pennsylvania; Adjutant, Lieutenant York. The captain of Company K, formerly a chaplain in Kentucky (Captain G. P. Riley), is thought to have preached in Bethel Church the previous Sabbath. There are several local preachers in the regiment; officers and men asked to be supplied with the Christian Recorder.

events.name: Rev. W. D. W. Schureman takes charge of Bethel; quarterly meeting
events.location: Bethel Church, Sixth St., Philadelphia
events.description: Notice that Rev. W. D. W. Schureman is appointed in charge of Bethel Church until the next conference (succeeding Rev. Stephen Smith's interim charge after Rev. J. P. Campbell's resignation). His first notice as elder in charge: Quarterly Conference Oct. 20; General Class Oct. 23; Quarterly Meeting Oct. 25; Love-feast Oct. 26, 1863.

events.name: Address by Rev. Samuel Harrison, chaplain of the 54th Massachusetts
events.location: Central Presbyterian Church (Rev. John B. Reeve), Lombard St., Philadelphia
events.description: On 'last Tuesday night' at 8 o'clock Rev. Samuel Harrison of Massachusetts, appointed by Gov. Andrew chaplain to the 54th Mass. Colored Regiment, spoke at Rev. Mr. Shreeves' Lombard St. church; Rev. Elisha Weaver opened with prayer. Harrison described being refused a cabin passage on the steamer from New York to Beaufort and ordered out of shelter as a deck passenger, until officers of 'the Third Colored Regiment, of Philadelphia' on board took up his case; his visits to Hilton Head, to Gen. Saxton at Beaufort and to the wounded of the 54th in Hospital No. 6; and the work of the missionary Rev. James Lynch. A collection was taken to aid him in fitting out. The paper prints 'Rev. Mr. Shreeves' Church'; this is Rev. John B. Reeve's Central Presbyterian Church.

events.name: Grand Tabernacle of Love and Charity (James H. Smith party): mass meeting called
events.location: New Masonic Hall, South Eleventh Street, Philadelphia
events.description: Mass meeting of the Past Officers and members of the Grand Tabernacle of the Independent Order of Brothers and Sisters of Love and Charity at their lodge room, Monday evening Oct. 19 at 8 o'clock, 'business of the greatest importance'; by order of the Grand Worthy Superior, James H. Smith. This is the party opposed to William Cooper's Grand Tabernacle (see Oct. 10); its Corresponding Committee's reply in the same issue (dated Philadelphia, Oct. 12) calls the Philadelphia Institute meetings of Sept. 14 and 18 an 'assumed grand body', irregular and unlawful, and promises the question will be brought before this special meeting.

events.name: Quarterly meeting at Jordantown, N. J.
events.location: Jordantown, N. J.
events.description: The editor crossed by the Market St. Ferry on Sabbath morning (Oct. 11) and walked most of the way. Bishop Nazrey preached in the morning and the editor administered the Lord's Supper; in the afternoon Rev. W. H. Jones ('Panorama') preached; a brother called on to exhort 'reared and pranced' and jumped from the pulpit, which the editor disapproved. The editor spoke on the church organ and literary matters. That evening at Bethel a minister from Baltimore preached.

events.name: Rev. W. D. W. Schureman introduced as Elder of Bethel; Bishop Payne presents Wilberforce
events.location: Bethel Church, Philadelphia
events.description: An unsigned correspondent reports that 'last Sabbath' (Oct. 18) a new Elder was introduced at Bethel in the midst of the conference year, a thing he believes never happened before in the church's history. Bishop Nazrey was present; Rev. W. D. W. Schureman preached from Matt. 21:28, a 'well-timed and creditable effort' on the duties of the minister and the subordinate departments of the church, some remarks received with loud responses; 'whether, when he comes to administer the law he will be so acceptable we shall see'. At 3 o'clock Bishop Payne presented the claims of Wilberforce University to a very full house; the object had not been announced and the collection was small (twenty-seven dollars); the Bethel Sabbath School contributed fifty dollars. Bishop Nazrey's notice in the same issue confirms the appointment in place of Rev. J. P. Campbell, orders Campbell to turn over his accounts and effects as District Book Steward to Schureman, attaches the Zion Mission to the Bethel station until Conference, and joins Norristown and Germantown to the city Mission under Rev. T. H. Cooper, 'sub. A. L. Stanford'. Nazrey's mail goes to Chatham, C. W., from Nov. 10 to Feb. 1, 1864, then to Pine St., Philadelphia.
attendees: Bishop, presented the claims of Wilberforce University
resigned Elder and District Book Steward (not present; named in the Bishop's notice)

events.name: Bethel Church Sabbath appointments; Bishop Payne at Union A. M. E.
events.location: Bethel Church, Sixth St., and Union A. M. E. Church, Coates St., Philadelphia
events.description: Bethel, Oct. 25: 10 o'clock Rev. A. L. Stanford; 3 o'clock Rev. J. R. V. Morgan; 7 1/2 o'clock Rev. Jacob Jay; W. D. W. Schureman, Elder. Same day at 3 p.m. Bishop D. A. Payne to preach at Union A. M. E. Church, Coates St., and present the claims of Wilberforce University; notice by A. L. Stanford, Minister.
attendees: preacher at Bethel; minister of Union A. M. E.
Bishop, at Union A. M. E.

events.name: Corner-stone laying, A. M. E. Church, Mount Holly, N. J.
events.location: Mount Holly, N. J.
events.description: Corner-stone to be laid Nov. 7, services at 11 o'clock with a collection for the church; Rev. Messrs. Moore and Woodlin expected; extra meeting on Sabbath the 8th. Notice dated Mount Holly, Oct. 21, 1863, by T. Gould, Minister in Charge.

events.name: Voyage of the 6th U.S. Colored Troops from Philadelphia to Yorktown
events.location: Philadelphia to Fortress Monroe and Yorktown, Va.
events.description: Letter of Capt. G. P. Riley (Company K), dated Yorktown, Oct. 19: the transport lay at Philadelphia eighteen hours after embarking, reached the breakwater on Friday in a storm, anchored with Morristown in sight, ran short of fresh water (salt water was distilled, 'such a beverage') and of cooked meat (five barrels of pickled pork steamed in the boiler); many were seasick. On Sabbath morning the 18th they were at Fortress Monroe, then ran up to Yorktown, disembarked, marched through the fort and encamped on the plains. 'We never lost a man or a dollar's worth of property.' The editor's notice calls Riley 'our esteemed friend and Christian patriot'.

events.name: West End Mission (A. M. E.) opening service
events.location: Hall at Broad and Lombard Sts., Philadelphia
events.description: The editor visited Brother Cooper 'on last Sabbath, at the opening of his Mission, at Broad and Lombard Sts.' and was pleased with the service and the attendance. Brother James Frisby preached at 3 o'clock. 'The Mission presents a promising field. There is quite an interesting Sabbath School attached to the Mission.' (Cooper is the Rev. Thomas H. Cooper, city missionary, of the Nov. 7 notice; only the surname is printed here.)

events.name: Grand Tabernacle of the U. O. B. S. L. C. of New Jersey created at Camden
events.location: Yeager's Hall, S. 3d St., Camden, N.J.
events.description: Delegations from the several tabernacles of the U. O. B. S. L. C. (United Order of Brothers and Sisters of Love and Charity) of New Jersey met in convention and created a Grand Tabernacle. Delegation from Mount Olive, No. 7: Josiah Cornelius, Andrew B. White, Shepard S. Sample, Thomas L. Brown, Rosanna Barnes, Lydia Hambleton, Sarah White, Sarah Watson, Adelia Moore, Mary Jackson. From Heart and Hand Tab., No. 20: James Stites, Charles Emery, Emma Brown, Alice Colen, Hannah Emery, Mary Bell, Anne Colen. From a third tabernacle (name illegible), No. 25: Edward Turner, Mary Rolman. Mount Sinai Tabernacle, No. 27: John H. Bean, Sarah Spearman, Gracey A. Julius, Susan Anderson, Rachel H. Lewis. (All delegate names are best readings of a blurred film and carry [VERIFY].) Called to order by Bro. A. B. White; Bro. J. Cornelius chairman pro tem., A. B. White secretary, Bro. Edward Turner chaplain pro tem. John H. Bean was chosen president of the convention and Thos. L. Brown secretary. A committee of seven nominated the officers of the Grand Tabernacle: G. W. S., John H. Bean; G. D. W. S., John E. Simpson; G. W. V. S., Sarah White; G. D. W. V. S., Eliza Bulaugh [VERIFY]; G. W. S., Elizabeth Parker; G. W. Conductor, Lydia Hambleton [VERIFY]; G. W. A. C., Sarah Watson [VERIFY]; G. W. I. S., Alice Colen [VERIFY]; G. W. O. S., Henry Rumsey; G. W. Chap., Edward Turner; G. W. R. S., Sheppard S. Sample; G. W. F. S., Andrew B. White [VERIFY]. The officers were elected and installed by the Rev. W. D. W. Schureman, G. W. S. of the U. O. B. & S. of L. & C. for the State of Pennsylvania. Signed Thos. L. Brown, Secretary.
attendees: G. W. S.; president of the convention

events.name: Eulogy on Mrs. Beulah Armstrong at Gouldtown
events.location: A. M. E. Trinity Church, Gouldtown, N.J.
events.description: Rev. Henry Davis delivered a eulogy on Mrs. Beulah Armstrong, born in Gouldtown in 1813, converted in her 18th year, a member of the A. M. E. Church in Gouldtown for fifteen years and then of the A. M. E. Church in South Camden. She married in her 25th year, lost her husband in August 1862, and died on the 7th of August, 1863, aged about 50 years and 3 months.

events.name: Presentation of a flag to the 3d Regiment U. S. Colored Troops at Sansom Street Hall
events.location: Sansom St. Hall, Philadelphia
events.description: 'On last Tuesday evening' the hall was filled to overflowing with colored and white people for the presentation of a flag to the 3d Regiment [regiment numeral as read; see flags] of the United States Colored troops. The flag was painted by Mr. Bowser, 'a colored man and an artist No. 1', by special order of the patriotic colored ladies of Philadelphia, who contributed the funds. Mr. John Quincy Allen, a graduate of the colored high school, was chosen by the ladies to present the flag in their behalf. Some two speeches were made before he spoke: Rev. Mr. Slicer, who has been chaplain in the army, and Mr. Walker. 'Next came our young (orator) J. Q. Allen, who delivered an address which was a credit to his head and heart.' Colonel Wagner, commander of Camp William Penn near Chelten Hills, made a brief speech. Mr. Wm. Nichols, 'a very staunch Abolitionist', delivered an excellent speech. 'This meeting was creditable to our race.'

events.name: Grand Tabernacle of Pennsylvania, Independent Order of B. & S. of L. & Charity: quarterly meeting
events.location: New Masonic Hall, S. Eleventh St., Philadelphia
events.description: Notice dated Philadelphia, Nov. 17th, 1863: the Quarterly Meeting of the Grand Tabernacle of the State of Pennsylvania of the Independent Order of Brothers and Sisters of Love and Charity will be held at the New Masonic Hall, S. Eleventh St., on Friday afternoon at 2 o'clock. All subordinate tabernacles in the city to attend; State tabernacles to send delegates, for whom the Grand Tabernacle will provide. By order of the Grand Worthy Superior, James H. Smith; attest, Nathaniel Wiggins, Grand Scribe.

events.name: Missionary Meeting at the West End Mission hall
events.location: Hall on Lombard street, near the south-east corner of Broad, Philadelphia
events.description: A Missionary Meeting with preaching at half-past 10 A. M. by the Rev. Joseph Smith, at 3 P. M. by the Rev. Elisha Weaver, and at half-past 7 P. M. by the Rev. Thomas H. Cooper, with a collection to aid the enterprise. 'There are great demands for a church in this section of the city. Come one, come all, and assist us in endeavoring to raise up a Zion out here.'

events.name: Bethel Church under repair; services in the basement
events.location: Bethel A. M. E. Church, Philadelphia
events.description: Bethel Church is undergoing extensive repairs at an outlay of some twelve hundred dollars or more; the congregation worships in the basement meanwhile and expects to resume services in the main audience room by the first of December, so that the church may present a respectable appearance when the General Conference assembles. In the same issue: Rev. J. P. Campbell (who resigned Bethel in September) has been placed in charge of a chapel in Baltimore vacated by Rev. Wm. H. Hunter, now an army chaplain; and A. L. Stanford corrects Bethel's Wilberforce apportionment to $664.40.

events.name: Wilberforce University: Philadelphia District committee apportions the second payment
events.location: Philadelphia Conference District
events.description: The committee on Wilberforce University appointed by the Philadelphia Annual Conference (Stephen Smith, president; Morris Hall, treasurer; A. L. Stanford, secretary; Willis Nazrey, J. P. Campbell and Henry Davis, committee) announces that the Baltimore District has made the first payment and that the Philadelphia District is expected to make the second payment of $3500 by the 10th day of March, 1864. With above 5000 members in the District, a small sum from each member would raise it. Ministers are to collect and forward to the treasurer (Brother Morris Hall) or the president, Rev. Stephen Smith. Apportionments are printed for Bethel, Union and Wesley A. M. E. Churches, Philadelphia, and for the Reading, Trenton, Freehold, Norristown, Camden, Salem, Woodbury, Frankford, Bordentown, Lancaster, Brunswick Station, Oxford, Snowhill, Riceville, Berks Co., Princeton, West Chester, Bridgeton, Penningtonville, Burlington and Cape May circuits (the dollar figures are too faint on the film to transcribe safely). The committee recommends bazaars, festivals, fairs or public contributions.

events.name: West End Mission of the A. M. E. Church opened at Broad and Lombard
events.location: Hall at the south-east corner of Broad and Lombard Sts., Philadelphia
events.description: Rev. Thomas H. Cooper, city missionary of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, has rented the hall at the south-east corner of Broad and Lombard Sts. for religious services every Sabbath at 10 A. M., 3 and 7 P. M., with a Sabbath School at 8 1/2 A. M. and 1 1/2 P. M. 'We need a church west of Broad St., to meet the westward march of society.' Cooper also signs, as minister in charge, a notice of revival meetings in the A. M. E. Church at Germantown (A. L. Stanford, elder).
attendees: city missionary; minister in charge at Germantown (Rev.)

events.name: Funeral of Rebecca C. Young at Bethel Church
events.location: Bethel Church, Philadelphia; burial at Olive Cemetery
events.description: Reported in Alfred M. Green's obituary letter (dated Philadelphia, Nov. 28, 1863; pages 2 and 3). Rebecca C. Young, wife of Jacob B. Young, Esq., died at or near Germantown on Aug. 8, 1863, aged 31 years, 1 month and 9 days, where she had gone to sew for a Mrs. Cameron and to recruit her health. Her first serious attack came in February 1862, in Walnut street near the residence of Brother Henry Brooks, who secured a carriage and conducted her home. Her sister, Mrs. Hannah Cornish, wife of the Rev. John C. Cornish, was buried on Nov. 27, 1862, the National Thanksgiving day. A member of Bethel Church for upwards of twenty years; of the Schureman Beneficial Society from its formation; of the Henderson Benevolent Society over eleven years; the writer thinks also of the I. O. of Good Samaritans and Daughters of Samaria; of Love and Charity from the organization of the Independent Order of Brothers and Sisters of Love and Charity; and nearly ten years an active member of King Solomon Tabernacle, No. 6. The letter reprints her letter of Aug. 15, 1860 from Delaware Water Gap (copied from the True Royalist of Sept. 27, 1860), sent with five dollars to one of the Philadelphia rescuers then confined in the Eastern Penitentiary for the attempted rescue. On the morning of Aug. 12, 1863 Bethel Church was filled to repletion; her body was conveyed from her husband's residence to the church; the pastor, Rev. Jabez P. Campbell, preached from Job 7:16, 'I would not live alway', followed by an exhortation by the Rev. J. B. Trusty, Elder of Big Wesley Church; the choir chanted a dirge; burial in the Olive Cemetery.
attendees: Elder of Big Wesley Church, exhortation (Rev.)

events.name: Grand Tabernacle of New Jersey, I. O. of Brothers and Sisters of Love and Charity: quarterly communication and election
events.location: Burlington, N.J.
events.description: Officers elected for the next twelve months, as printed: Brother E. Waterman [VERIFY initial], G. W. S.; Sister Mary A. Carlisle, G. W. V. S.; Bros. B. F. Brown, G. W. R. S.; Paul Hammond, G. W. T.; E. Mann [VERIFY], G. W. C.; Sister Comfort Powell, G. W. C.; Sister Maria Griffin, G. W. A. C.; Bro. James Mann, G. W. I. S.; Brother S. H. Handy, G. W. O. S. A preamble and resolutions followed: having learned by rumor and newspaper publications that difficulties exist in the Grand Tabernacle for the State of Pennsylvania, arising from a difference of opinion on the constitutionality of an election held at Westchester on Friday, Sept. 4, 1863, which divided that Grand Tabernacle and set up another body claiming the same jurisdiction, the New Jersey body suspends all relations with both Pennsylvania sections until officially informed, and forbids its Tabernacles to admit members of Pennsylvania Tabernacles under penalty of suspension. Signed E. Mann, G. W. S., and B. F. Brown, G. W. R. S.

events.name: Rev. Jabez P. Campbell preaches for the city mission in the West Section
events.location: Hall on Lombard St., near the south-east corner of Broad St., Philadelphia
events.description: Announced by Thomas H. Cooper, City Missionary: Rev. Jabez P. Campbell to preach at 3 o'clock P.M., with a collection for the missionary enterprise. A second notice in the same issue calls a Quarterly meeting in the same hall 'on the third Sabbath of this month, Dec. 28th, 1863' (so printed; the third Sabbath was Dec. 20), signed T. H. Cooper, Preacher in Charge, and A. L. Stanford, Elder.

events.name: Festival of the ladies of Wesley A. M. E. church, Hurst St.
events.location: Wesley A. M. E. church, Hurst St., Philadelphia
events.description: A festival to run night and day for one week from Dec. 24, to assist in paying the debt of the church, of which Elder J. H. Smith [VERIFY middle initial] is pastor. A prize cake holding two gold rings to be cut on the last night. Season tickets 25 cents, single tickets 10 cents. (The Dec. 26 issue reports on the 'Wesley Fair'.)

events.name: Second Reformed Dutch Church of Freehold presents its communion service to the A. M. E. Church of Freehold
events.location: Freehold, New Jersey
events.description: The A. M. E. Church of Freehold reports a protracted meeting (forty mourners, about twenty-six professing) and a concert that raised thirty-seven dollars, twenty-five paid on the church debt. The Second Reformed Dutch Church of Freehold (white) gave its old communion service of three plates, two cups and one pitcher, with a resolution signed by its pastor and clerk; the reply of thanks, dated Freehold, Dec. 8th, 1863 (day digit faint), is signed in behalf of the A. events.name: Funeral discourse for Chrissy A. Brown, A. M. E. Union Church, Cape May
events.location: A. M. E. Union Church, Cape May, New Jersey
events.description: Rev. Henry Davis preached from Romans 8:18 on the life of Chrissy A. Brown, born in Middle township, Cape May, Nov. 17, 1819; joined the M. E. Church in Cape May in 1837 and remained in it for years until she and most of the colored members withdrew in 1845 and applied as a body to Rev. Henry Davis for admission into the A. M. E. Church, into which they and their church were received. She taught the infant class of the Sabbath School fifteen successive years. She died Nov. 29, 1863, aged 44 years and 15 days as read (age digits faint), taking leave of her mother and sisters.

events.name: William Still put off a city passenger car between Germantown and the city (streetcar discrimination)
events.location: City passenger railway from Germantown, Philadelphia
events.description: William Still's letter to the Philadelphia Press, dated Philadelphia, Dec. 11, 1863, reprinted by the Recorder. Obliged to go out to Camp William Penn on business, he took the North Pennsylvania Railroad and reached the ground about 11 o'clock. Unable to return the same way without waiting two and a half hours, he walked to Germantown, missed the steam cars by about five minutes, and took the city passenger cars with a man in his employment (white). The conductor took the fare for both and then invited him to 'step out on the platform': 'It is against the rules'; asked who objected, 'It is the aristocracy'. Still answered that it was a cruel rule, that he believed this the only city of note in the civilized world where a decent colored man is not allowed to ride in a city passenger car; that even the cars built in Philadelphia for New Orleans had accommodations for colored people inside; and that a petition some time back was freely signed by hundreds of the most respectable citizens, among them Bishop Potter and Hon. Horace Binney, and some railway presidents. The conductor named the president of the road (name blurred, reads 'Mr. Whartman'). Still told him he paid taxes; it was of no avail. He rode on the platform on a bitter cold day; it began to snow, and he got off and walked the rest of the distance, 'satisfied that nowhere in Christendom could be found a better illustration of Judge Taney's decision in the Dred Scott case'. He notes that every colored man, woman and child of the 25,000 [as read] inhabitants of the city is daily liable to this treatment, and recalls two instances: a venerable old minister of the Gospel, going to his home at Frankford one dark, cold, rainy night last winter, was killed while occupying the only place on the platform assigned to colored people; and two elegantly dressed young women going home from a lecture, one of whom was thrust out of the car by physical force, though her father pays several hundred dollars taxes annually and keeps his horse and carriage. The Recorder's preface calls the treatment 'a crying shame upon the managers of these roads'.
attendees: ejected to the platform; author of the letter

events.name: Rally day at Bethel Church to pay the renovation debt; Bible presented by Dr. Armstrong
events.location: Bethel Church, Philadelphia
events.description: 'Last Sabbath' before the issue of Dec. 26. At 10 A.M. Elder Schureman, the ministers, trustees and members marched in procession from the basement up the south aisle to the altar and pulpit and round to the north aisle, singing the jubilee hymn. At half past ten Rev. Thomas Kennard of Canada preached from Ps. lxviii. 13; at 2 P.M. Rev. A. L. Stanford preached from Ps. lxviii. 16. Elder Schureman then called the class leaders forward, thirty in number. Dr. Armstrong 'of this city' had promised a Bible worth twenty-five dollars to the leader who raised the most money in proportion to the number in his class. The highest amount was given by Rev. James Frisby and class, $95 (69 members as read); next, Brother Henry Gordon, $80, with 42 members; Gordon would have got the Bible, but the Delmonico Association of young men, of 30 members, laid down one hundred dollars and took the prize. The whole amount raised is printed as 'over $7000' (so read; possibly $700). Dr. Armstrong presented the Bible to the young man with an address to 'Brother Schureman and friends of Bethel Church', printed in full. The report shows Schureman in charge of Bethel after J. P. Campbell's resignation.

events.name: Grand Tabernacle, I. O. of Brothers and Sisters of Love and Charity: quarterly session
events.location: Their Hall, South Eleventh St., Philadelphia
events.description: Quarterly Session of the Grand Tabernacle of the I. O. of B. and S. of L. and C., at their Hall, South Eleventh St., Philadelphia, dated December 4th, 1863, 2 o'clock P.M. Brother James H. Smith (first printed 'James M. Smith') acting grand worthy superior; Sister Sarah Young, grand worthy Vice. Minutes of the called meetings of Oct. 12th and 19th approved. On motion of brother Henry Brooks the September minutes were corrected to read J. B. V. Morgan instead of J. P. Morgan. The appointment of brother R. H. Gleaves as grand Deputy was declared null and void, 'it having been set forth by his own testimony that he favored the Rebellion against this grand body'; brother Henry Gordon was appointed in his place. Reports of Tabernacles: Jerusalem No. 2 not present; Brooks No. 8, 94 cts.; Prudence No. 7, $1.20; King Solomon No. 6, $1.80; Celestial No. 7 (so printed), $2.51; Olive Branch No. 8, 80 cts.; Smith's Tabernacle, $1.12 (numbers and sums as read, several faint). The acting scribe, in place of brother Wiggins, received $1.50. The committee to secure the books and property of the grand Body from brother Wm. H. Longfellow reported and was discharged; copies secured by brother Green were deposited in the Archives; a bill of $1.10 from brother Brooks for visiting Tabernacles at Thornburg was paid. Brother James H. Smith stated that Prudence Tabernacle had money to pay to No. 6 but was not certain who were its legal representatives; the grand officers, with brother John G. Dutton, worthy superior of No. 6, were asked to visit and set the matter right. Signed J. H. Smith, G. W. S.; A. E. Johnson, Scribe pro tem. Evening session, 7 1/2 P.M.: No. 5 officially reported defunct; Jerusalem Tabernacle No. 1 asked time to adjust difficulties over members 'supposed to be on the fence in relation to the seceders'. Committee to purchase books: A. M. Green, Henry Brooks, Anna Cooper. Committee to secure the books and property from brother Wm. H. Longfellow: A. M. Green, Joseph Robinson, James W. Kemp [VERIFY]; the same to confer with Atheneum Tabernacle No. 13 on the trouble now existing in the order. The revision committee reported forty-three Degree books. A resolution to expel brother Wm. Cooper was tabled. A. M. Green was paid $1.50 as scribe for the evening. Prudence Tabernacle was permitted to use the Regalia at their next grand Anniversary. Finance committee: brother Brooks, brother Morgan and sister Frances Sebastian. Signed James H. Smith, G. W. S.; A. M. Green, G. Worthy Scribe pro tem.
attendees: former officer holding the books and property
grand worthy scribe pro tem.; committees

events.name: Third U. S. Colored Troops before Fort Wagner: killed and wounded; pay protest
events.location: Morris Island, South Carolina
events.description: Two letters from the Third U. S. C. T., the regiment raised at Camp William Penn. Wm. H. Johnson, Co. A (page 3, to his father, November 1863) lists the killed and wounded while digging in the intrenchments before Wagner, as read: Co. A: Corporal Powell, died of a shell wound; Private Andrew Jackson, killed in action; Corporal Denny, wounded; Sergeant G. Allen, died; Private Levi T. Brown, died. Co. D: Sgt. Hardy, wounded; Corporal Locke, killed in action; Privates Jas. Gray and A. Rockhold, killed; Jas. Finley, wounded slightly; Jas. Bird, killed in action. Co. I: C. D. Lamb, wounded (lost right arm); S. Sweeny, wounded (leg); F. A. Villies, George Carter and C. Thompson, died in hospital. Co. G: Privates Goddard and James Weeks, wounded. Co. E: Privates H. Jackson, died; C. Johnson, wounded; S. Mayhew, killed in action; W. Williams, wounded. 'Co. W' (so printed): Private D. Jones, killed in action; McGwire, T. Jackson, B. Bradley and J. Jones, wounded. Co. H: James Roe, reported dead. He praises Col. Tilghman and asks to be remembered to the ladies of the Sanitary Commission; an N.B. reports two officers lost by disease. Sergeant H. S. Harmon (page 2, December 1863) reports that the men voted the two medals of honor promised by General Gillmore to each company (in his company Privates George Reed and William Roberts, 'both Lancaster County boys'), and that the regiment, called up again for payment, was offered only seven dollars in cash with three reserved for clothing, which over two-thirds of the men refused with the remark that they 'could not see it'.
